The defensive layers the app applies out of the box, and what each leaves to you. The
settings named here are described in [CONFIGURATION.md](/reference/configuration/); what the app
stores and logs about callers is in [PRIVACY.md](/reference/privacy/).

- **Security headers** (`Content-Security-Policy`, `X-Content-Type-Options`,
  `X-Frame-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`). Everything the page loads or connects to
  (the Debug pane's websocket included) is same-origin, so the CSP allows nothing else.
  The policy is:

  ```
  default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';
  font-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'self'; object-src 'none';
  base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'
  ```

  **`script-src 'self'` runs only script files this app serves**: no inline `<script>`,
  no `onclick=`-style handler, no `javascript:` URL, no `eval`. No page carries any: the
  editor's code is served from `/static`, and the data a page needs (the flow, for the
  editor) travels in a `<script type="application/json">` block, which the browser never
  executes. So text that gets into a page (a flow's description, a component's prompt)
  can't run as script there even if its escaping were ever wrong, and couldn't send what
  it read anywhere but this app. `style-src` keeps `'unsafe-inline'` because the
  in-browser Tailwind build writes its styles at runtime; injected CSS can restyle a page,
  not run script. A proxy in front of the app that adds a CSP of its own must not loosen
  this one, and one that injects a script (analytics, a "you are on staging" banner)
  needs it served as a file, or the browser refuses it. Script URLs carry a `?v=` content
  hash, so a browser never runs a cached editor from a previous release.
- **Request size limit**: bodies over `MAX_REQUEST_BYTES` (1 MiB) are rejected with `413`.
- **Rate limiting**: per-IP `RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE` on the UI/API (webhooks and `/health`
  exempt). This is a **per-process** first line of defence; for cross-instance limits and
  **webhook-flood protection**, front the instance with a gateway (the platform layer).
- **Global error handler**: unhandled exceptions are logged server-side and return a
  generic error (never a stack trace).
- **Authentication**: session login (`AUTH_ADMIN_*`, plus an optional view-only
  `AUTH_READONLY_*` account) for standalone use, or **delegated auth**
  (`TRUSTED_USER_HEADER`) where a fronting gateway authenticates and passes the identity in
  a header (the seam a hosting platform uses). Trusted-header mode is safe **only** when
  the gateway is the sole route to the app and strips the header inbound; or, better,
  also set `TRUSTED_USER_HEADER_SECRET`: the identity header is then honoured only on a
  request carrying the same value in `X-Trusted-Proxy-Secret`, which the gateway adds
  (and the app strips before anything else sees it).
- **Sign-in bounds**: a session ends after `SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT` seconds without a
  request (the cookie's `Max-Age` is the same, so the browser drops it too), and the
  moment its account's **password is changed** (every session made with the old one,
  including a stolen cookie in active use). The cookie is `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`, and
  `Secure` on an https deployment.
- **Guessing limits**: an address that fails `LOGIN_MAX_ATTEMPTS` sign-ins is refused
  for `LOGIN_LOCKOUT_SECONDS`, before its password is even checked. Guessing spread over
  many addresses runs into `LOGIN_GLOBAL_MAX_ATTEMPTS`, the shared count for every
  browser that has never signed in here; reaching it pauses sign-in for those browsers
  and logs an `ERROR`. A browser that *has* signed in before carries a signed
  `known_browser` cookie (sent only to `/login`, bound to its account and current
  password) and is counted on its own instead, so a campaign can't lock the real admin
  out. None of this replaces a long random password: the app warns at startup about any
  password under 16 characters (webhook basic auth included, which has no limit at all).
- **Flows can't read the manager's secrets**: a component may reference `{{headers}}` to
  inspect the inbound request, so the credential-bearing headers (`Authorization`,
  `Proxy-Authorization`, `Jambonz-Signature`, `Cookie`, `X-Trusted-Proxy-Secret`) are
  masked before a flow sees them.
- **Bounded outbound responses**: the `http_request` node streams and abandons a response
  past `HTTP_REQUEST_MAX_BYTES`, and never follows redirects (a redirect would be resolved
  after the SSRF check).
- **Webhook authenticity**: `WEBHOOK_SECRET` enables verification of the
  `Jambonz-Signature` header Jambonz sends on every webhook (`t=<ts>,v1=<hex>`,
  HMAC-SHA256 over `"{timestamp}.{body}"`, the same scheme Jambonz's own SDKs verify).
  The signed timestamp is checked against a 300 s tolerance, so captured requests can't
  be replayed later. The value is your account's webhook secret from the Jambonz portal
  (`GET /Accounts/{Sid}/WebhookSecret`); comma-separate several for multiple accounts or
  rotation. Alternatively (or additionally), `WEBHOOK_BASIC_AUTH_USER` +
  `WEBHOOK_BASIC_AUTH_PASSWORD` require, on webhook routes only, the basic-auth
  credentials configured on the application's two webhooks in Jambonz. With neither,
  anyone who can reach the port can run any flow, and hand it its env-var values, which
  arrive on that same inbound hook: an HTTP Request node whose URL starts with
  `{{env_vars.API_BASE}}` then sends the token it carries to whatever host they name.
  Every start logs a `SECURITY:` error until one is set.
- **The env-var schema is public by Jambonz's design.** Jambonz fetches a flow's
  application env-var schema with an `OPTIONS` request to its webhook and signs nothing
  on it, so anyone who can reach the port can ask (webhook basic auth, if set, still
  applies). The answer shows which flow names declare env vars, and each variable's name,
  description and **default, unless it is obscure**. Keep internal URLs and anything
  else you'd rather not publish in an obscure variable, or set them in the Jambonz portal
  with no default in the flow.
- **"Obscure" hides a value here, not from Jambonz.** An obscure env var is masked in the
  Debug and Simulate panes, shown as `••••••••` to the read-only account, never logged,
  never in the `OPTIONS` schema, and dropped from exports and version downloads. But its
  value rides on the call (`customerData`, echoed on every webhook), so Jambonz, its
  portal's call traces (OpenTelemetry `http.body`) and its call records have it in clear.
  A *default* for one is also stored in clear in the flow, its version history and every
  backup, and a save warns about it: set secrets in the Jambonz portal. See
  [PRIVACY.md](/reference/privacy/).
